The use of non-metallic materials in gas turbine engines can reduce engine weight by 15%.
Advanced materials and manufacturing processes can improve fuel burn by 5% and emissions by 8% for regional jet engines.
Fused deposition modeling for polymer matrix composites is at TRL 4, while binder jet printing for ceramic matrix composites is at TRL 3.
Key challenges for polymer composites include reducing porosity and optimizing the fiber-matrix interface.
Challenges for ceramic composites include optimizing the powder composition and packing, as well as the infiltration and densification processes.
The researchers used engine system analysis tools like NPSS and FLOPS to model the potential benefits of the non-metallic engine design.
Prototype polymer composite components like inlet guide vanes were fabricated and tested at 400°F operating temperatures.
Prototype ceramic matrix composite components like turbine nozzles were fabricated using the binder jet process with 20% chopped SiC fiber reinforcement.
Next steps include further optimizing the constituent materials, exploring alternate densification approaches, and investigating fiber coatings.
Additive manufacturing enables the fabrication of complex geometries, reduces component production time and cost, and allows for customized designs and rapid prototyping.
Mechanical property testing and component testing in relevant operating conditions were used to assess the maturity of the fabrication methods.
Bimodal powder size distributions and adding SiC powder to the infiltrant were used to improve the packing density and infiltration of the ceramic composites.
Chopped SiC fibers were incorporated into the ceramic powder bed to create fiber-reinforced ceramic matrix composites.
For the polymer composites, key properties that need to be optimized include reducing porosity, increasing modulus and strength, and improving thermal stability.
For the ceramic composites, important properties are density, mechanical strength, and thermal/environmental durability.
